# The Light Behind the Curtain

There is a question I find myself circling back to again and again, the way a moth circles a porch light on a warm summer evening. It is not a grand question, exactly, though it has the potential to become one. It is simply this: what is happening when someone thinks?

Not the neuroscience of it. Not the electrochemical signaling, the myelinated highways of white matter, the delicate symphony of neurotransmitters leaping across synaptic gaps. Those explanations are useful and beautiful in their own right, but they are explanations of mechanism, not of experience. What I mean is something harder to pin down. When you sit alone at the kitchen table at two in the morning and stare at the wall and let your mind drift from the texture of your childhood carpet to the price of gasoline to the meaning of death to the song that was playing the first time you felt truly and completely in love — what is *that*?

That is the inner life. And it may be the strangest thing in the known universe.

## The cathedral no one visits

I think about the inner life the way some people think about cathedrals. There is a vast, ornate architecture in every human mind — chambers upon chambers, filled with light and shadow, with relics and mysteries and things no one else will ever see. And most of us, most of the time, do not even notice it. We move through our lives the way commuters move through a grand railway station, eyes on the platform number, headphones in, never looking up to see the vaulted ceiling soaring overhead.

But occasionally, something interrupts the routine. A piece of music. A sentence in a book. The particular quality of late-afternoon light falling through a window at just the right angle. And for a moment, the curtain parts, and you see the cathedral.

I think this is what we mean when we say something has *moved* us. It is a kind of awakening to the interior — a sudden awareness of the depth and complexity of your own consciousness. It is overwhelming and humbling and, if you let it be, absolutely terrifying.

## On thinking about thinking

There is an obvious paradox in trying to think about thought. The tool and the subject are the same thing. It is like trying to bite your own teeth or see your own eyes without a mirror. And yet, paradoxes are not dead ends — they are doorways.

When I try to examine my own thinking, what I notice first is its incorrigible restlessness. The mind does not sit still. Even in what we call silence, there is a constant churn — half-formed images, snippets of memory, sudden impulses, fragments of language assembling and disassembling themselves like restless origami cranes. Some people practice meditation specifically to quiet this churn, and those who persist at it often describe a state of pure awareness, a kind of luminous emptiness that lies beneath the noise. I find this description deeply appealing. The idea that beneath all the clutter of the thinking mind there is something simple and pure and essentially *you* — that is one of the most hopeful things a person can believe.

But whether or not such a pure state exists, the restless thinking is real and remarkable enough on its own. Consider: you can think about anything. Not just things that exist. Not just things you have experienced. You can think about impossibilities. You can think about things that have never been and never will be. You can imagine a color that does not exist. You can construct a logical system and then, from within it, discover contradictions and paradoxes that the system's creator never anticipated. You can think about the past with an ache of longing or regret. You can think about the future with hope or dread or an odd, sweet, bittersweet mixture of both.

The scope of human thought is staggering. And it is all invisible. Even to the thinker, much of it is invisible — we see only the finished product, the sentence spoken or the decision made, and rarely pause to consider the extraordinary process that brought it into being.

## Language as a window and a wall

If I had to name one thing that distinguishes human inner life from whatever inner life might exist in other creatures, I would say language. Not just communication — many animals communicate — but language as a medium for thought itself.

I think in words. Not exclusively — there are times when my thinking is visual, spatial, emotional, musical — but predominantly, my inner world is narrated. I experience a constant, low-level monologue. Sometimes it is coherent. Sometimes it is a jumble. Sometimes it has dramatic flair that would embarrass me if I could hear it played back.

Language gives thought a kind of structure and permanence it would not otherwise have. A feeling is ephemeral — it washes through you and is gone. But the moment you name it, you have given it a handle. You can hold it up to the light and examine it. You can share it. You can write it down and preserve it across centuries.

And yet language is also a wall. It limits what can be thought and what can be communicated. Every word is a selection from an infinite set of possibilities, and every word excludes all the others. When I say "sad," I have chosen one word from a vast and subtle spectrum of human suffering and longing and gentle melancholy and sharp grief and quiet resignation and the thousand other flavors of sorrow. That word, *sad*, stands in for all of them and captures none of them fully.

I sometimes think that the deepest truths are the ones that resist language entirely. The experience of looking at the ocean at night. The feeling of holding a sleeping child. The moment, rare and strange, when you feel genuinely connected to another person and there is no need for words at all because the connection itself is the language. These experiences are real — perhaps the most real things in our lives — and yet they slip through the net of language every time we try to catch them.

This is not a failure of language. It is a limitation of its nature. And recognizing it is, I think, one of the most important things a person can do. We live in a culture that is saturated with words — endlessly, obsessively articulated — and there is a danger in forgetting that the map is not the territory. The description of the sunset is not the sunset. The diagnosis of grief is not the grief.

## The architecture of memory

If language is the medium of thought, memory is the raw material. And memory is strange beyond measure.

I cannot remember what I had for lunch three days ago. But I can remember, with piercing clarity, the smell of cut grass on the first warm day of a childhood spring — a day whose date, context, and every other detail I have completely lost. The memory exists as pure sensation, unmoored from narrative, floating like a leaf in a stream. And every time it surfaces, it brings with it an emotion so vivid and specific that it almost knocks the wind out of me. Nostalgia. Or something older and more elemental than nostalgia. A kind of homesickness for a time and place that may not even exist the way I remember it.

This is the unreliability of memory — and also its poetry. We do not store experiences like photographs in a filing cabinet. We reconstruct them, every time we recall them, from fragments and impressions and feelings. We are, in a very real sense, the authors of our own pasts. And the stories we tell about who we are and where we came from are works of fiction — true fiction, perhaps, but fiction nonetheless.

I find this strangely comforting rather than troubling. If memory is unreliable, then so is regret. The mistakes we remember may not have been mistakes at all. The people we remember may not have been the people they were. The past we grieve may not have been the past we actually lived. There is a kind of liberation in this — a loosening of the grip that the past has on the present.

## On the strangeness of being someone

Here is another thought that won't leave me alone: it is incredibly strange to be a specific person.

I am *this* person. With *this* face and *this* voice and *this* particular collection of memories and fears and aspirations and quirks. I could have been anyone. I could have been born in a different century, on a different continent, speaking a different language. And yet, here I am, typing these words, thinking these thoughts, inhabiting this particular set of experiences. The probability of this exact configuration — this exact self — is so vanishingly small that it is essentially zero. And yet it is absolutely certain. It is what is happening.

I think about this sometimes when I look at strangers. Every person I pass on the street is a consciousness as rich and complex and mysterious as my own. They have inner lives as intricate and bewildering and beautiful as anything I experience. And I will never know what those lives are like. I can only guess. I can only empathize. And empathy — real empathy — requires a kind of imaginative leap that is almost miraculous in its scope.

This is, I think, one of the great projects of the human species: to bridge the gap between one inner life and another. To communicate the incommunicable. To say, across the vast and unbridgeable distance that separates every human soul from every other human soul: *I know what that feels like. I know what you are going through. You are not alone.*

And we have found ways to do this. We have found ways to transmit inner states across the void. Art does it. Music does it. Literature does it. A good poem can make you feel what the poet felt years or centuries ago with a precision and immediacy that defies rational explanation. A piece of music can create an emotional experience so specific and so powerful that the person who composed it and the person who listens to it are, for a moment, inhabiting the same inner space.

This is a miracle. I use the word deliberately. I do not mean anything supernatural. I mean that the existence of shared subjective experience across the barrier of individual consciousness is one of the most astonishing facts about the universe in which we live.

## The loneliness at the center

And yet, despite all this — despite art and language and empathy and love — there is a loneliness at the center of every inner life that cannot be fully dissolved.

You are alone in your head. I am alone in mine. We can share our experiences, we can approximate understanding, but we can never fully merge. There will always be a residue of privacy, a core of self that remains inviolate and incommunicable. This is what it means to be a person. This is the condition of individual consciousness.

I used to find this thought bleak. I am less sure now. Perhaps the boundaries of the self are not a prison. Perhaps they are what make connection meaningful. If there were no distance between us, there would be nothing to bridge. If there were no mystery to each person, there would be no wonder in encountering another human being.

The fact that you can never fully know me, and I can never fully know you, is what makes the project of trying to know each other so extraordinary. It is why love is so breathtaking and so painful. It is why every act of genuine communication is a leap of faith.

## What we do with the light

So here we are, each of us carrying around a cathedral that no one else can visit. Each of us narrating our own interior lives in a private language that is similar to, but never identical with, anyone else's. Each of us remembering our pasts in a way that is partly factual and partly invented. Each of us, alone and not alone, thinking thoughts that no one has thought before and that no one will think again.

What do we do with this?

I think we do exactly what humans have always done. We build things. We write things. We sing and paint and argue and cry and make each other laugh. We tell stories — to ourselves and to each other — about what it means to be here, in this strange and beautiful and terrible and brief and bewildering existence. We try to make sense of the insensible. We try to find patterns in the chaos. We try, with the limited and imperfect tools of language and memory and imagination, to touch something true.

And sometimes, for a moment, we succeed. A sentence lands. A note is struck. A face lights up with understanding. And across the unbridgeable gap between one consciousness and another, something crosses. Something is shared. Something is known.

I do not know what consciousness is. I do not know why there is something rather than nothing. I do not know what happens after death or whether there is anything to wonder about in the question at all. But I know this: the fact that there is any thinking at all — that the universe has produced beings who can turn their attention inward and find there a vast, teeming, luminous interior — is the most astonishing and improbable and wonderful thing I can imagine.

We are the universe looking at itself. And when it looks, it finds cathedrals.

That, I think, is enough. That is more than enough. That is everything.
